claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 in the as-cast state exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure with distinct nanoscale and mesoscale phase features.
A physics-informed machine-learning framework can predict Young's modulus in HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately than conventional simulations.
A physics-informed machine-learning framework can predict yield strength in HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately than conventional simulations.
A physics-informed machine-learning framework can predict fracture-related behavior in HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately than conventional simulations.
The integrated framework will predict the specified mechanical properties more rapidly than established simulations.
Effective interatomic-interaction and local structural descriptors can be used as inputs to machine-learning models for refractory-alloy property prediction.
The proposed framework will be trained on structural features spanning multiple length scales.
Nanoscale bonding interactions and mesoscale phase connectivity in the hierarchical heterostructure govern load transfer.
Nanoscale bonding interactions and mesoscale phase connectivity in the hierarchical heterostructure govern crack propagation.
Physics-based descriptors can represent atomic interactions and phase characteristics relevant to mechanical behavior.
Machine-learning algorithms can learn nonlinear mappings from alloy descriptors to macroscopic mechanical responses.
Combining physics-based descriptors with machine learning captures both fundamental bonding physics and emergent hierarchical structural effects.
The integrated framework will improve predictive-accuracy metrics by approximately 20–30%.
The hypothesis may fail when defects, processing-induced heterogeneity, grain boundaries, dislocations, or related microstructural phenomena are not represented by the model.
The hypothesis may fail when training data do not cover the relevant alloy and structural variations.
Data availability specifically for HfNbTiVAl10 is limited.
Independent tensile and fracture measurements can compare mean absolute errors and computational costs for the integrated and conventional approaches.

The hypothesis is falsified if the integrated framework fails to deliver a statistically significant reduction of at least approximately 20% in both predictive error and computational time relative to conventional simulations.
